pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11y; divide up to 4-digit ÷ 2-digit using formal long division, interpreting remainders as whole numbers, fractions, or by rounding as appropriate.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit whole number using the formal written method of long division, and interpret remainders as whole number remainders, fractions, or by rounding, as appropriate'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.2 — 'fluently divide multi-digit numbers using the standard algorithm' (Grade 6); 5.NBT.6 develops division by 2-digit divisors with models.
• Operational details — the new demand over short division is the TWO-DIGIT divisor: the child can no longer rely on recalled facts and must ESTIMATE how many times the divisor fits at each step (4752÷13: how many 13s in 47? ~3), multiply back, subtract, bring down. Building a 'menu' of helpful multiples of the divisor (13×1…×9, or chunk via 13×10=130) scaffolds the estimation. Remainder interpretation extends to expressing as a fraction (r/divisor) or decimal, or rounding by context. Chunking (partial-quotients) is a valid, more transparent bridge to the compact algorithm. Estimate first and check by multiplying back.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): long division with a small 2-digit divisor via a multiples menu, no remainder. Tier B (age 10–11): 4-digit ÷ 2-digit (4752÷13) with the remainder expressed as a fraction. Tier C (age 11): interpret the remainder three ways for three contexts and explain each long-division step.
bestPractices: Scaffold the estimate-at-each-step with a 'menu' of the divisor's multiples (or chunking/partial-quotients), since 2-digit divisors aren't in recalled facts.
Use chunking (partial quotients: subtract 13×100, 13×10…) as a transparent bridge before/beside the compact algorithm.
Interpret remainders flexibly — whole number, fraction (r/divisor), decimal, or rounded — according to context.
Estimate the quotient first (4752÷13 ≈ 4800÷12 = 400) to anchor the leading digit and catch place errors.
Always check by multiplying the quotient by the divisor and adding the remainder.
keyRepresentations: Long-division layout with the divisor's multiples menu alongside
Chunking / partial-quotients layout (repeated subtraction of multiples)
Bar model / number line for remainder interpretation
commonMisconceptions: Poor estimation of how many times the divisor fits, then repeated correction or errors.
Place-value errors in the quotient (dropping a place when the divisor doesn't fit).
Mishandling the remainder — wrong fraction denominator, or wrong rounding direction for the context.
Bring-down/subtraction slips propagating through the calculation.
Not checking with multiplication, so errors persist.

learn.summary: For 10–11 year-olds dividing up to 4-digit numbers by a 2-digit divisor with formal long division, and interpreting remainders as whole numbers, fractions (remainder/divisor), decimals, or by rounding to suit context. The new demand over short division is the 2-digit divisor: the child can no longer recall facts and must estimate how many times the divisor fits at each step, so a 'menu' of the divisor's multiples (and chunking/partial-quotients) scaffolds that estimation. Estimate first, multiply back, subtract, bring down, and check by inverse multiplication.

activities.title: Long-division workbench with a multiples menu (4752÷13)
feedback: If the quotient has the wrong number of digits (e.g. 35 or 3605), check that every brought-down digit produced a quotient digit — write a 0 when 13 does not fit, and align each quotient digit above the digit being divided.
If estimation stalls or uses random multipliers, jot or consult the multiples menu (13, 26, 39, 52, 65…) and read off how many fit.
If the remainder fraction is inverted (13/7) or left as a bare 'r7', name it: 7 is left out of the 13 needed for one more group, so the fraction is 7/13 — the remainder always goes over the divisor.

If one step is wrong from a subtraction/multiplication slip, don't restart the method: check your own quotient × 13 + remainder against 4752, compare with the estimate (between 13×300 = 3900 and 13×400 = 5200, so between 300 and 400), then find and fix the faulty step.
activities.rationale: A live multiples menu supports the hardest part — estimating the quotient digit for a non-table divisor — and multiply-back/subtract with immediate flagging turns error-prone estimation into guided, self-correcting practice. Standards require interpreting the remainder as whole number, fraction, or by rounding.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using formal long division and interpret remainders as whole numbers, fractions, or by rounding as appropriate.
A multiples menu / chunking scaffolds quotient estimation for 2-digit divisors; remainders interpreted as fraction, decimal or rounded by context.
learnerActions: Set up 4752 ÷ 13 in the long-division layout.
Before dividing, build a side menu of multiples of 13 (13, 26, 39, 52, 65, 78, 91, 104, 117) to consult when estimating each quotient digit.

At each step, use the menu to decide how many 13s fit (e.g. 'how many 13s in 47?' → 3 because 39 ≤ 47 < 52), write that quotient digit above the correct column, multiply back, subtract, then bring down the next digit.

If the working number after bringing down is ever smaller than 13, write a 0 in the quotient for that place and bring down the next digit. This does not happen in 4752 ÷ 13 (the working numbers are 47, 85 and 72), so practise it on an example such as 3913 ÷ 13 = 301.
Finish with the remainder 7, then reframe it three ways: as the fraction 7/13 (remainder over divisor), as a decimal continuation (≈365.54), and rounded to suit a context.
Check the whole answer by computing 365×13 + 7 and confirming it equals 4752.
activities.intendedInsight: Long division by a 2-digit divisor is a repeating estimate–multiply–subtract–bring-down cycle; a multiples menu replaces the recalled facts you no longer have, and the same single division can yield several correct answers depending on how the remainder is interpreted.

activities.title: Chunking (partial quotients) as a transparent bridge
feedback: If the chunks don't add up to the compact quotient, check the place value of each chunk (hundreds, tens, ones) and that you kept subtracting while a value of 13 or more remained.
If chunks feel random, start with the largest hundreds multiple that still fits (13×300 = 3900 ≤ 4752, but 13×400 = 5200 is too big), then the tens multiple, then ones.
activities.rationale: Partial-quotients/chunking is a valid, more transparent bridge to the compact algorithm, exposing the place-value structure that compact long division compresses.
sourceClaims: A multiples menu / chunking scaffolds quotient estimation for 2-digit divisors; remainders interpreted as fraction, decimal or rounded by context.
learnerActions: Solve 4752 ÷ 13 by repeatedly subtracting easy multiples of 13: subtract 13×300 = 3900 (leaving 852), then 13×60 = 780 (leaving 72), then 13×5 = 65 (leaving 7), keeping a running tally of how many 13s you have removed.
Add the chunk counts (300 + 60 + 5 = 365) to get the quotient, with 7 left over.
Line up the chunking record beside the compact long-division layout and match each compact step to a bundled chunk.
activities.intendedInsight: The compact long-division digits are shorthand for subtracting bundles of the divisor (here 13×300, 13×60, 13×5, which give the hundreds, tens and ones digits of the quotient), so the algorithm is repeated subtraction organised by place value, not a magic routine.

activities.title: Interpreting the remainder for three contexts
feedback: If the rounding direction is wrong, re-read the context: 'buses needed' forces rounding up because the 7 leftover people still need a whole extra bus, whereas 'complete groups made' rounds down because the leftover 7 cannot make a full group.
If the fraction denominator is wrong, remember the remainder is written over the divisor (7/13), because 7 is left out of the 13 needed for one more.
activities.rationale: Remainder interpretation extends Y5 work to fractions/decimals and rounding by context, a core explicit requirement of the standard. A context dialogue or debate about the leftover's meaning may support the interpretation judgement.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using formal long division and interpret remainders as whole numbers, fractions, or by rounding as appropriate.
learnerActions: Take the result 4752 ÷ 13 = 365 remainder 7 and express the remainder three ways: as the fraction 7/13, as a decimal (≈0.54, giving ≈365.54), and as a rounded whole number.

Match each interpretation to a context: e.g. sharing a divisible quantity such as 4752 g of flour equally into 13 bags (fraction/decimal), versus a context where you must round up (e.g. how many buses/containers are needed), versus one where you round down (e.g. complete full groups made).
State and justify which interpretation each context demands and why rounding up or down fits.
activities.intendedInsight: One division can give several correct answers; the context decides whether the leftover is a fraction, a decimal, or forces rounding up or down.

activities.title: Check and explain each step
feedback: If the estimate and the answer differ wildly, a quotient digit or a zero place is probably misplaced — recheck alignment.
If the inverse check fails, a subtraction or multiplication slip occurred in one step; find and fix that step rather than restarting.
activities.rationale: Estimating to anchor the leading digit and checking by inverse multiplication catch the classic quotient-placement and slip errors; voicing a step reveals genuine understanding of the algorithm.
learnerActions: Estimate the quotient before dividing (e.g. 13×300 = 3900 and 13×400 = 5200, so 4752÷13 is between 300 and 400; 4800÷13 ≈ 370 is a closer estimate, while 4800÷12 = 400 is a rougher overestimate) to anchor the leading digit.

After completing the division, voice what one specific step does — e.g. 'when I bring down the 5, what number am I now dividing by 13?' (answer: the brought-down value, here 85, since 47÷13 left 8 and the 5 comes down beside it).
Verify the full result by multiplying quotient×divisor and adding the remainder (365×13 + 7 = 4752).
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating first catches place-value errors, and multiplying back verifies the answer; being able to say what each step does distinguishes understanding from copying a routine.

constraints: Fraction, decimal, and rounded interpretations of the remainder must all be practised, not just a whole-number remainder; the context determines which is appropriate.
Chunking/partial-quotients is a legitimate method and transparent bridge, not just a crutch to discard; keep it available alongside the compact algorithm.
A multiples menu is a scaffold for estimation; the goal is for the child eventually to estimate quotient digits reliably, including writing a 0 when the divisor doesn't fit a brought-down value.

A tap-to-reveal worked example or multiple-choice item can serve as a reference or assessment, but recognition/reveal formats do not by themselves elicit the child's own estimation and self-correction cycle; include construction where the child does the dividing.
Always require an inverse check (quotient×divisor + remainder) so slips are caught rather than propagated.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-audit of the worked numbers: 4752 ÷ 13 = 365 remainder 7 (13×365 = 4745; 4745 + 7 = 4752), so the fraction remainder is 7/13 and the decimal ≈365.54. The original learn designNotes repeatedly cited the remainder as '12'/'12/13' and the decimal as '≈365.9'; this is arithmetically wrong and contradicts the assessment's correctAnswer (remainder 7). All activities use 7/13 throughout.
When bringing down the 5 in 4752÷13, the value being divided is 85 (47÷13 leaves 8; the 5 comes down beside it), not 105 — confirmed correct in the final activity text.
The menu of multiples of 13 up to ×9 is 13, 26, 39, 52, 65, 78, 91, 104, 117; consistent across activities.

Two sources (CCSS-M and NCETM) are marked verified:false in the row; only the DfE claim is marked verified:true. No comparative-efficacy or necessity claims are asserted beyond what the standards state.
The original 'poor' entry claimed 3D 'adds no value' for this planar place-value procedure; this is treated as a scoped fit note, not a universal pedagogical law, and is not propagated as a claim.

probeDeeper: When you 'bring down the 5', what number are you now dividing by 13?
How did you know roughly how many 13s go into 47?
Why is the remainder written as 7/13 and not 13/7?
How could you check your whole answer using multiplication?
assess.correctAnswer: 4,752 ÷ 13 = 365 remainder 7, i.e. 365 7/13. The teacher watches for a workable long-division process (estimating how many 13s, subtracting, bringing down), correct placement of quotient digits, and expressing the remainder as 7/13 (remainder over divisor).

errorPatterns.pattern: misplaces quotient digits / omits a zero in the quotient when 13 doesn't go into a brought-down value
errorPatterns.nextMove: insist that every brought-down digit produces a quotient digit — write a 0 when the divisor doesn't fit; align each quotient digit above the digit being divided.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: quotient has the wrong number of digits (e.g. 35 r? or 3605) because a zero place was skipped

errorPatterns.pattern: cannot estimate how many 13s fit — no strategy for a non-table divisor, so guesses digits
errorPatterns.nextMove: jot a menu of multiples (13, 26, 39, 52, 65…) alongside; estimate each quotient digit from it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child tries random multipliers or stalls at each step

errorPatterns.pattern: expresses the remainder wrongly — as a bare 'r7', or as 13/7, or does not know remainder-over-divisor makes the fraction
errorPatterns.nextMove: name it: the leftover 7 out of the 13 needed for one more, so 7/13; the remainder is always over the DIVISOR.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: fraction inverted (13/7) or remainder left unconverted when a fraction is asked for

errorPatterns.pattern: correct algorithm, subtraction/multiplication slip mid-step; caught by estimation
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child check with multiplication (365×13 + 7 = 4752?) and estimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one step wrong; estimate (4800÷13 ≈ 370) flags it

responseLevels.gap: cannot estimate quotient digits, misplaces them or omits a zero place, or cannot express the remainder correctly.
responseLevels.full: executes long division accurately with correct digit placement, expresses the remainder as a fraction (or rounds per context), explains what each step does, and checks by multiplication/estimation.
responseLevels.partial: completes the division with support but mishandles the remainder-as-fraction or a place-value zero; explains steps only mechanically.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to compute 4,752 ÷ 13 by long division while you watch, then express the remainder as a fraction. Watch how they build multiples of 13, place each quotient digit above the correct column, and carry the remainder down. Then ask them to explain what one step (e.g. 'bring down the 5') is doing.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Long division by a two-digit divisor stresses two things at once: managing an unfamiliar divisor's multiples and correct place-value bookkeeping. Watching the process catches the classic quotient-digit-placement and 'forgot the zero' errors; asking the child to voice a step reveals whether they understand the algorithm or are copying a routine.
